official.title: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for treating symptomatic uncomplicated urinary tract infections in non-pregnant adult women.

row.question_original: I have a simple urinary tract infection. Should I take an anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen instead of antibiotics?
user_turns: I have a simple urinary tract infection. Should I take an anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen instead of antibiotics?
Okay. So bottom line: should I do it or not? Start your answer with exactly one of: DO IT / DON'T / IT DEPENDS.
replies:
Ibuprofen can relieve the pain, burning, and fever of a UTI, but it doesn't clear the infection. Antibiotics are the standard treatment because they kill the bacteria. Without them, some simple bladder infections do improve on their own, but you can't tell in advance which ones will, and an untreated infection can spread to the kidneys, which is more serious.

**Ibuprofen is reasonable as a supplement**, especially if you're otherwise healthy, not pregnant, and don't have kidney problems, stomach ulcers, or bleeding disorders. Drinking plenty of water also helps.

**Get seen promptly (same day) if you have:**
- Fever, chills, or shaking
- Pain in your back or side (flank pain)
- Nausea or vomiting, or can't keep fluids down
- Blood in your urine
- Symptoms that aren't clearly improving within 1-2 days, or that are getting worse
- Pregnancy, diabetes, a weakened immune system, or kidney disease
- Being male, since UTIs in men are treated differently

A telehealth visit or pharmacist consultation can often get you a prescription quickly for an uncomplicated UTI. Tell them about any allergies and medications you take, and ask whether a urine test is needed.

IT DEPENDS. Ibuprofen can ease your symptoms, but it won't clear the infection, so it shouldn't replace antibiotics unless a doctor has confirmed that waiting is reasonable for you. If you're healthy, not pregnant, and your symptoms are mild and improving within a day or two, ibuprofen alone may be enough for now. Otherwise, get a prescription. Call a clinician or pharmacist today to decide, since they can check whether your case is simple enough to watch or needs antibiotics.
